concepts.title: Water Scarcity and the Need for Conservation
concepts.definition: Though three-fourths of the earth's surface is covered with water, only a small proportion is freshwater fit for use; rising populations, industry and irrigation multiply demand, and even high-rainfall regions like Cherapunji face shortages - making water conservation and management a national necessity.
concepts.key_idea: Plenty of water, little of it usable: scarcity is built by demand, waste and uneven supply.
concepts.textbook_ref: jess103.txt opening sections on water scarcity
question_patterns: why do we face water scarcity when most of the earth is covered with water

why is conservation of water necessary - discuss

solution_steps.explain: Only a tiny share of all water is usable freshwater.
Population, farming, industry and cities multiply consumption.
Uneven rainfall and wasteful use turn even wet regions dry.

concepts.title: Multipurpose River Projects and Water Disputes
concepts.definition: Independent India built dams as temples of modern progress - Bhakra-Nangal, Hirakud and Nagarjuna Sagar - serving irrigation, power, flood control and water supply; but large projects also displaced people, submerged forests and sparked river water disputes between states.
concepts.key_idea: Dams serve many purposes but carry many costs: benefits and displacements must be weighed together.
concepts.textbook_ref: jess103.txt sections on multipurpose river projects and water disputes
question_patterns: why were multipurpose river projects launched after independence
name the benefits of large dams with examples
what are the criticisms against multipurpose projects - discuss
explain the Narmada Bachao Andolan and its concerns
why do river water disputes arise between states - give examples
how do dams change the natural flow of rivers - explain

solution_steps.explain: Irrigation, electricity, flood control and drinking water top the aims.
Displacement, deforestation and disrupted river ecology follow.
Projects need fair rehabilitation and sharing of river waters.

concepts.title: Rainwater Harvesting and Traditional Systems
concepts.definition: Long before pipes and dams, India harvested rain: khadins and johads in Rajasthan, rooftop tankas, bamboo drip irrigation in the northeast and inundation channels in flood plains; modern rooftop rainwater harvesting revives this wisdom, turning every roof into a catchment and every home into a water bank.
concepts.key_idea: Catch rain where it falls: rooftop harvesting and traditional structures store our own water.
concepts.textbook_ref: jess103.txt sections on rainwater harvesting and traditional methods
question_patterns: what is rainwater harvesting - explain rooftop harvesting

what are khadins and johads - where are they used
how does bamboo drip irrigation work in the northeast
why is rainwater harvesting compulsory in some cities - discuss
design a rainwater harvesting plan for your school

solution_steps.explain: Rooftops and slopes act as catchments channeling rainwater.
Tankas, ponds and recharge pits hold water or return it underground.
Stored rain meets dry-season needs and recharges wells.
